notes: The assessment must match the branch. An imaging change needs its modality, baseline, acquisition time, units and protocol threshold; tissue response needs the sampled sites, adequacy and definition. A change in one lesion is not a complete patient-level assessment, and a blood assay measures circulating material. Predicted pathological complete response is not the surgical finding itself, and a negative biopsy describes only the tissue submitted. Strategy benefit needs a comparator, recurrence or survival endpoint, follow-up and harms. No universal response percentage supplies permission to omit treatment.

In the 2024 I-SPY2.2 phase 2 report, 106 participants received datopotamab deruxtecan with durvalumab in the first block for high-risk stage II or III breast cancer. Subtype-specific algorithms used serial magnetic resonance imaging volume change and core biopsy to redirect later blocks, including earlier surgery for participants predicted to have a high probability of complete pathological response. The endpoint was assessed at resection. This was a defined research strategy, not permission to cancel surgery or a demonstration of equivalent long-term survival.

Postoperative adaptation has different comparisons. CREATE-X selected residual HER2-negative invasive disease after chemotherapy; OlympiA selected high-risk germline BRCA1/2-associated HER2-negative disease; EA1131 did not demonstrate that platinum was noninferior or superior to capecitabine in its residual basal-subtype comparison. Those studies do not directly test adding their medicines to the complete pembrolizumab sequence. Risk, a plausible mechanism and eligibility do not independently establish added benefit.

A baseline marker selecting a medicine differs from an on-treatment response rule. Response adaptation changes a participant's later treatment; response-adaptive randomisation changes assignment probabilities for future participants. A trial can use both. A safety-driven hold or substitution is a further distinct decision: favourable cancer response does not settle whether treatment can safely continue, or prove a changed course equivalent to the original one.

Consider a fictional early-surgery checkpoint requiring both a specified MRI criterion and an adequate negative biopsy. The scan meets its criterion, but the biopsy is inadequate. The combined AND rule is not met, because an uninterpretable input cannot be replaced by the favourable scan. This exercise supplies no numerical cutoff or treatment instruction; correct branch logic remains separate from evidence that acting on the rule improves clinical outcomes.

records.name: Active surveillance and observation
records.tldr: Deliberately not treating a cancer yet, but checking it regularly with blood tests, scans or biopsies and treating only if it shows signs of progressing. Standard for low-risk prostate cancer, small kidney masses and several other slow conditions.
records.summary: Active surveillance avoids or defers the harms of treatment for cancers unlikely to cause trouble: Grade Group 1 prostate cancer (ProtecT showed no survival penalty at 15 years), small renal masses, papillary thyroid microcarcinoma, low-risk DCIS (COMET), smouldering myeloma and early-stage CLL, and stage I testicular cancer after orchiectomy. It differs from watchful waiting, which forgoes curative intent. 'Surveillance' also describes the scheduled follow-up after curative treatment (CT, ctDNA, MRI in small-cell lung cancer instead of prophylactic cranial irradiation), and after complete response in organ-preservation strategies (SANO in oesophageal cancer).

records.name: Curative intent vs palliative intent
records.tldr: Curative intent means treatment aims to eliminate cancer durably. It names the goal, not a guarantee; the same medicine can be used with different goals.
records.summary:
Curative intent is a documented aim of durable cancer elimination, not a laboratory result or an individual probability of success. A destination analogy describes a goal; it does not mean that effort determines the outcome. Type and extent of disease, evidence, feasible and safe options, and personal priorities shape the plan.

A treatment can aim to cure, reduce recurrence, control growth or relieve symptoms. Palliative anticancer intent and palliative care are different: symptom, comfort and quality-of-life support can accompany treatment aimed at cure. The number of visits, intensity and side effects do not identify the goal. Complete remission describes the absence of detectable signs under the assessment used, not proof that cancer can never return.

notes: Surgery treats selected tissue, radiotherapy a planned volume and systemic therapy reaches sites through the body, without ensuring equal exposure or sensitivity everywhere. Systemic treatment can aim at cancer too small to detect. In nonmetastatic breast cancer, local and systemic treatments can contribute to a curative plan. Surgery and radiotherapy can also aim at disease control or symptom relief; location alone does not establish intent. Neoadjuvant treatment comes before the main treatment and adjuvant treatment after it; recurrence-reduction treatment can follow surgery when no tumour is visible. Sequence depends on the plan rather than a universal order.

For metastatic breast cancer the usual goals are control, longer life and symptom relief, but this statement is not a rule for every metastatic cancer or every selected clinical situation. Chemotherapy can contribute to cure, lower recurrence risk, slow growth or relieve symptoms. Shrinkage alone does not show a greater chance of durable cure. A proposed change needs evidence for the actual decision, along with safety and the person's priorities.

Assess effects using the relevant imaging, pathology, symptoms and defined recurrence or survival endpoints, with their clocks and duration of follow-up. A negative scan, pathological complete response or a fixed number of years does not guarantee that every cancer cell is absent. A recurrence does not prove every earlier treatment lacked benefit. Remission describes an observed decrease or disappearance of signs and symptoms. NCI distinguishes it, including complete remission, from the stronger claim that cancer will never return; observed group outcomes do not determine one person's future.

Consider a fictional person who has surgery, no visible disease afterwards, planned adjuvant treatment and support for nausea. Nausea care or a palliative-care consultation does not by itself change a documented curative goal. Palliative care can begin during curative treatment and addresses symptoms, function and quality of life; it is not synonymous with hospice or with abandoning anticancer treatment. Ask separately what the plan aims to do and what has actually been measured.
